items.title: Operation Northwoods
items.summary: A Top Secret memo the Joint Chiefs of Staff sent to Defense Secretary Robert McNamara on 13 March 1962, listing staged incidents that could serve as pretexts for US military intervention in Cuba. The ideas included a fake Communist Cuban terror campaign in Florida and Washington, a faked attack on a civilian airliner and blowing up a US ship in Cuban waters; Kennedy rejected the proposals.
items.credit: Joint Chiefs of Staff (signed by Gen. Lyman L. Lemnitzer)

facts.claim: The Joint Chiefs gave 'Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba' to Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara on 13 March 1962; its pretexts included a fake Communist Cuban terror campaign in the Miami area, other Florida cities and Washington, faking a Cuban attack on a civilian jetliner and a 'Remember the Maine' incident blowing up a US ship in Cuban waters.
The Assassination Records Review Board released about 1,500 pages of once-secret military records on Cuba on Tuesday 18 November 1997, including the pretext of sinking a boatload of Cuban refugees.
The Northwoods document was made public on 18 November 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board, and President Kennedy rejected the proposals.
The National Archives holds the JCS composite document 'Plan for U.S. Military Intervention in Cuba Codenamed Northwoods', with memorandums on pretexts to justify US military intervention in Cuba.

items.title: U-2 Photo of San Cristobal Missile Site
items.summary: Annotated U-2 reconnaissance print of MRBM Field Launch Site San Cristobal No. 1 in western Cuba, labeling erector-launcher equipment, eight missile trailers and tent areas. Photos from this 14 October 1962 flight were the first photographic evidence of Soviet offensive missiles in Cuba and set off the Cuban Missile Crisis.

facts.claim: The National Archives caption reads 'MRBM Field Launch Site, San Cristobal #1' and says this photo provided the first photographic evidence of Soviet offensive missile deployment in Cuba; the record is dated 14 October 1962 and the print was received from the Defense Department's public affairs office (OASD-PA).

On the morning of 14 October 1962 a U-2 piloted by Air Force Major Richard D. Heyser photographed western Cuba; the photos produced the first verified evidence of Soviet offensive missile sites, near San Cristobal.
US officials showed the reconnaissance photographs at the UN Security Council on 25 October 1962.

items.title: Report on Plots to Assassinate Castro
items.summary: The CIA Inspector General's 1967 internal report on agency plots to kill Fidel Castro, written for Director Richard Helms after President Johnson ordered an investigation. It covers poisoned cigars, a diving suit dusted with fungus, a booby-trapped sea shell and the use of a gambling syndicate; first released in censored form in the 1990s, this copy comes from the National Archives' December 2022 release.
items.credit: CIA Office of Inspector General (J. S. Earman)

facts.claim: After a 7 March 1967 Drew Pearson column, President Johnson directed CIA Director Richard Helms to investigate; Inspector General J. S. Earman sent Helms the report in installments beginning 24 April 1967.
The National Archives released record 104-10213-10101, '1967 IG Report on Plots to Assassinate Fidel Castro', 143 pages, on 15 December 2022.

The report's contents list contaminated cigars, a skin diving suit (dusted inside with a fungus causing Madura foot), a booby-trapped sea shell, the gambling syndicate operation and Project AMLASH; its cover memo carries a 'CIA Historical Review Program Release as Sanitized 1997' stamp.
A 1996 book edition of the report notes that it was declassified in 1994.

items.title: ExComm Meeting Tape, October 16, 1962
items.summary: Secret White House recording of the first meeting on the Soviet missiles in Cuba, held hours after Kennedy learned of the U-2 photos: photo interpreter Arthur Lundahl briefs him on the pictures and his advisers start debating air strikes and an invasion. The Kennedy Library first released the tape, with large parts withheld, in October 1983.
items.credit: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library (White House recording, Tape 28); audio file via the Miller Center, University of Virginia

facts.claim: McGeorge Bundy told Kennedy about the U-2 photographs at 8:45 a.m. on 16 October 1962 and Kennedy called his principal advisers to a meeting; the recording is Tape 28, digital identifier JFKPOF-MTG-028, and its transcript opens with 7.5 pages on the analysis of the U-2 photographs.

The National Archives holds the transcript of the 'Off the Record Meeting on Cuba', 16 October 1962, 11:50 a.m. to 12:57 p.m., described as the first meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Security Council.

The Miller Center offers this recording (jfk_028_1.mp3) as 'Meeting on the Cuban Missile Crisis', 16 October 1962, with participants including Arthur Lundahl, Sidney Graybeal, Dean Rusk, Robert McNamara and Robert Kennedy.
On 26 October 1983 the Kennedy Library released a tape and transcript of the two 16 October 1962 meetings, with large portions blocked out after national security review.

items.title: Khrushchev Letters to Kennedy
items.summary: President Kennedy's office file of Nikita Khrushchev's letters from 23 October to 19 December 1962, with Russian originals, Moscow embassy telegrams and State Department translations, including the 26 October letter about the 'knot of war'. The October letters were declassified in November 1973; the rest, including Robert Kennedy's memo on his 27 October meeting with Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin, followed between 1991 and 1998.
items.credit: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library (President's Office Files); translations by U.S. Department of State
items.license: US government records, public domain; the Soviet originals are official state correspondence

facts.claim: The folder 'Cuba: Security, Missile Crisis: Khrushchev correspondence, 1962: 23 October-19 December' holds Khrushchev's letters to Kennedy about Soviet missiles in Cuba and Robert Kennedy's memo to Dean Rusk on a meeting with Ambassador Dobrynin.

Khrushchev's 26 October 1962 letter, sent as Moscow embassy telegram 1101, says 'the more the two of us pull, the tighter that knot will be tied'; its translations were printed in the Department of State Bulletin of 19 November 1973.

The folder's withdrawal sheet and stamps show the October letters declassified 21-27 November 1973, Robert Kennedy's 30 October memo (on his meeting with Dobrynin on Saturday 27 October) declassified in April 1991, and the later letters in January 1992 and June 1998.

items.title: Low-Level Photo of San Cristobal Site 1
items.summary: Low-altitude reconnaissance photo of Soviet medium-range ballistic missile Site 1 at San Cristobal, labeled to show fuel and oxidizer tank trailers, a missile shelter tent, a missile erector and tracked prime movers. It was taken on 23 October 1962 and released by the Department of Defense the same year.

facts.claim: The US Information Agency's 1962 photo file caption reads 'Low level photograph of the San Cristobal Mid Range Ballistic Missile site #1 erected by the Soviet Union' and gives the source as the U.S. Department of Defense (the caption's date '1-23-62' is a slip for 23 October).
A CIA print of San Cristobal MRBM Site 1 with the same labels (oxidizer tank trailers, missile shelter tent, missile erector, cable lines) is dated 23 October 1962.

items.title: Bay of Pigs Inspector General Report
items.summary: CIA Inspector General Lyman Kirkpatrick's October 1961 internal investigation of the failed April 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, with annexes of planning papers. It blamed the CIA's own poor organization, staffing and management rather than Kennedy's cancellation of the D-Day air strikes, and stayed secret until the National Security Archive obtained its release in 1998.
items.credit: CIA Office of Inspector General (Lyman B. Kirkpatrick)

facts.claim: The survey covers the project from 1959 to the April 1961 invasion, warns against blaming the President's cancellation of the D-Day air strikes, and finds the fundamental cause was the Agency's failure to give the project appropriate organization, staffing and direction; it has five annexes of policy and planning papers.
Written in October 1961 by CIA Inspector General Lyman Kirkpatrick, the report was made public by the National Security Archive on 22 February 1998 after a two-year Freedom of Information Act effort.
This file is part 1 of 2 of the CIA Historical Review Program release of the 'Inspector General's Survey of the Cuban Operation and Associated Documents', mirrored from the CIA Reading Room.

items.title: The Cuba Project (Operation Mongoose)
items.summary: Brig. Gen. Edward Lansdale's 18 January 1962 program review for Operation Mongoose, the covert campaign to help Cubans overthrow Fidel Castro's Communist government from within. It assigns 32 numbered tasks to the CIA, State, Defense and USIA, from intelligence collection to propaganda and sabotage; first published in 1997, this copy comes from the National Archives' May 2023 release.
items.credit: Brig. Gen. Edward G. Lansdale, Chief of Operations, Cuba Project

facts.claim: FRUS prints Lansdale's 'Program Review by the Chief of Operations, Operation Mongoose' dated 18 January 1962, with the objective 'to help the Cubans overthrow the Communist regime from within Cuba' and Tasks 1 through 32.
FRUS 1961-1963 Volume X (Cuba, January 1961-September 1962) was published by the Government Printing Office in 1997.
The National Archives released record 202-10001-10172, 'The Cuba Project', dated 18 January 1962, on 11 May 2023, with bracketed portions withheld by the Joint Staff.

rejected.reason: jfklibrary.org returns a Cloudflare 403 to scripts and archive.org has no copy of the October 1962 meeting tapes (its JFK meeting tapes stop at Tape 26A); used the Miller Center MP3 of Tape 28, which needs a browser User-Agent and a millercenter.org Referer.

rejected.reason: Offered only as EPUB/MOBI; the static PDF path returns 403. Used the scanned Kennedy Library folder of the original letters instead.

rejected.reason: Its PDF link returns an HTML page; only 11 separate JPGs exist.

rejected.reason: 181 separate GIF/JPG page images with no PDF; kept it as the source and used the 15-page National Security Archive PDF of the key memo.
